result: A large multi-site reference cohort was assembled from 82 sites with N=58,836 individuals aged 2-100 years, split equally into training (N=29,418) and test sets (N=29,418) stratified by site. Only first visits were included for longitudinal datasets, and stratification by site (not study) was used to address scanner confounds.
evaluation: Claims C1, C14-15, C34-37 provide consistent and explicit documentation of the sample composition, splitting procedure, and rationale. The stratification approach is well-justified with appropriate citations (C37), and the data splitting methodology is clearly described using standard tools (scikit-learn).

result: A manually quality-checked (mQC) subset of N=24,354 individuals from 59 sites was created for validation, combining manual QC by the authors with ABCD consortium QC. For the full sample, automated QC using the Freesurfer Euler Characteristic was employed. Model performance metrics were nearly identical between the full test set (automated QC) and mQC test set.
evaluation: Claims C2, C16, C39-42, C56, C61-63 collectively document a rigorous multi-pronged QC approach. The use of Euler Characteristic is well-supported by citations (C41-42), the manual QC procedure is explicitly described, and the comparison between QC methods (C56) validates the automated approach. The conservative threshold for automated QC (C63) addresses potential concerns about false exclusions.

result: The models were applied to a transdiagnostic psychiatric sample (N=1985 from 24 sites) to demonstrate clinical utility. Z-statistics from normative deviations provided stronger case-control effects than raw data for most diagnostic groups, and individual-level deviations provided complementary information to group effects. Clinical variation was widespread in a fine-grained manner across disorders.
evaluation: Claims C3, C17, C22-23, C29, C50-53, C57 provide converging evidence for clinical utility. The sample is well-characterized (C17), the analysis approach is clearly defined with appropriate thresholds (C50-52) and matched controls (C53), and the results demonstrate both improved case-control detection (C22) and individual-level heterogeneity (C23, C29) supported by prior work.

result: Model transferability was demonstrated using a transfer dataset from OpenNeuro.org (N=546 from 6 sites not in training). Pretrained models and code are shared online with Google Colab access, eliminating installation barriers and providing straightforward directions for transferring to new sites.
evaluation: Claims C38, C26, C64-65 document both the technical demonstration of transferability (C38) and the practical implementation for community use (C64-65). The transfer dataset provides independent validation, and the Google Colab implementation addresses accessibility concerns. The claim of easy transferability (C26) is supported by both methodological citations and empirical demonstration.

result: Normative models were implemented using Bayesian Linear Regression with likelihood warping (sinarcsinsh/SHASH distribution) in Python 3.8 with PCNtoolkit v0.20. Models used age, sex, and site (fixed effects) as covariates, with B-spline basis expansion for non-linear age effects and L-BFGS optimization. Freesurfer v6.0 was used to extract cortical thickness from the Destrieux parcellation and subcortical volumes.
evaluation: Claims C43-44, C46-49, C59-60 provide comprehensive methodological documentation with appropriate citations. The modeling approach is well-established (C46 cites Jones & Pewsey 2009, Dinga et al. 2021, Fraza et al. 2021), software versions are specified (C43, C59), and the choice of fixed vs. random effects is justified with prior work (C47-48). The preprocessing pipeline is standard and well-cited (C59-60).

result: The models explain up to 80% of variance out-of-sample across cortex and subcortex, with lifespan trajectories aligning with known patterns of development and aging. Model performance was consistent between automated and manual QC approaches.
evaluation: Claims C21, C55-56 report model performance metrics with appropriate validation. The explained variance (C21) is substantial and reported out-of-sample. The alignment with known developmental patterns (C55) is supported by relevant citations (Ducharme et al. 2016, Gogtay et al. 2004, Tamnes et al. 2010), and the consistency across QC methods (C56) validates the approach.

result: Sex differences in brain structure are most pronounced for large-scale features (mean cortical thickness, total gray matter volume) and manifest as a shift in mean with the same trajectory shape for both sexes, as determined by sensitivity analyses with sex-specific models.
evaluation: Claims C19-20 describe sex effects with supporting visual evidence (Figure 1C) and sensitivity analyses. The finding that sex effects are primarily mean shifts (C20) is based on empirical comparison of sex-specific models, providing appropriate validation of the modeling approach that uses sex as a covariate.

result: The models provide spatially specific estimates across 188 brain regions, offering high anatomical specificity for discriminating conditions, predicting outcomes, and stratifying subtypes. The models can handle non-Gaussian distributions and generate individualized fingerprints for clinical stratification.
evaluation: Claims C24-25, C28, C58 describe key capabilities of the approach. The number of regions (C28) is explicitly stated, the non-Gaussian modeling capability (C25) is supported by methodological citations, and the utility for clinical stratification (C24, C58) is demonstrated in the clinical validation (Figure 2). However, C58 is implicit rather than directly demonstrated.

result: Prior work (Bethlehem et al. 2021) modeled only global features (total brain volume) which has limited utility for stratifying clinical cohorts. The current work addresses this limitation by providing spatially specific estimates across 188 brain regions.
evaluation: Claims C12-13, C27-28 accurately characterize prior work and position the current contribution. The limitation of global features for clinical stratification (C13) is a reasonable inference supported by the demonstrated heterogeneity across disorders (C29). The citation to Bethlehem et al. 2021 is appropriate and the contrast is clearly articulated.

result: The dataset has unavoidable sampling bias from aggregating existing data, likely drawn predominantly from WEIRD societies. UKBiobank contributes 59% of the full sample. Freesurfer was not adjusted for very young ages (2-7 years), requiring caution when applying models to this age range.
evaluation: Claims C30-33 transparently acknowledge important limitations. The WEIRD bias (C31) is appropriately cited (Henrich et al. 2010), the UKBiobank dominance (C32) is explicitly quantified, and the Freesurfer limitation for young ages (C33) is clearly stated. These are honest assessments of methodological constraints that appropriately temper interpretation.

result: Normative modeling, established as an effective technique for individual-level neuroimaging inferences, is motivated by the role of atypical brain development trajectories in many disorders and associations between brain tissue and cognitive decline. However, a hurdle to widespread application is the lack of well-defined reference models across the lifespan.
evaluation: Claims C4-11 provide appropriate background and motivation, all supported by relevant citations. The historical context (C4), methodological foundation (C5-6), clinical rationale (C7-10), and identification of the gap (C11) are well-documented. These claims accurately represent prior work and establish the need for the current study.
